newsitem.title: USA: Morgan Stanley's Wien sees U.S. markets overvalued.
newsitem.headline: Morgan Stanley's Wien sees U.S. markets overvalued.

text.p: The U.S. stock market is about 12 percent overvalued, Byron Wien, chief U.S. investment strategist for Morgan Stanley, said on Monday.
Speaking on CNBC television, Wien said he based his valuation on a model involving interest rates and the Standard & Poors 500 index.

However, Wien said the overvaluation was not a cause for alarm because the index can become "egregiously overvalued." For example, it was about 40 percent overvalued in 1987, just before a severe correction, he said.

"But if you pay attention to it, eventually it tends to go back to fair value," said Wien, who had forecast a 1,000 point drop in the Dow Jones Industrial Average last year, but later backed away from that forecast.
"Now it's overvalued, but, you know, it's at 12 percent. That's not the end of the world. It can get much more overvalued."
Based on his model, Wien said the market had been seven percent undervalued in early December when Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspaon warned about shares' "irrational exuberance."
"The market has gone up and interest rates have gone up and that is why the overvaluation has swelled."
The Standard & Poors 500 index, which measures the average performance of 500 widely held stocks, closed down 2.31 points at 811.34 on Tuesday.
